Abstract The current scenario of the global halal market shows that it is a very profitable venture, as it is targeted to attain $3.2 trillion by 2024. This certainly signifies its substantial economic potential in various sectors such as food, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, tourism, and logistics. Halal certification is certainly beneficial for boosting international trade and foreign investment, as well as creating jobs specifically for SMEs. This study is an extension of existing research as it analyses halal certification from 2003 to 2022, to reveal three main phases: initial exploration (2003-2010), increased interest (2011-2015), and growth (2016-2022). The market reached its peak of research in 2020, which further reflects its increasing significance. This research highlights how halal certification is instrumental in assisting growth by ensuring compliance with Islamic principles and fulfilling rising demand. The aspects covered in this study are consumer behaviour, certification processes, ethical considerations, and industry opportunities, thus providing insights for policymakers, researchers, and practitioners on utilising halal certification for economic advancement and discerning potential research areas. Keywords: halal, standard, consumer, behaviour, economy 1. Introduction Halal certification plays a crucial role in ensuring compliance with Islamic dietary laws and facilitating market access. It is a stamp of approval that assures customers that products and services meet the required Islamic standards, thereby providing them with peace of mind and trust in halal offerings. It is particularly important for Muslim consumers worldwide who look for assurance that the products they consume are aligned with their religious beliefs. Halal certification also enables corporations to approach domestic and international markets, specifically in Muslim-majority countries and areas with large Muslim populations. Without proper certification, businesses may face challenges in promoting their products to these markets, thereby impeding their market access and growth opportunities (Ghazali et al., 2023). There is enormous economic potential in the halal industry, and it should not be overlooked. The global halal market has shown significant growth and is targeted to attain substantial values. For example, the halal market was valued at over $2.3 trillion in 2018 and is projected to reach approximately $3.2 trillion by 2024 (Nor et al., 2023). This increase signifies the increasing demand for halal products and services globally. The halal industry encompasses diverse sectors, including food and beverages, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, tourism, and logistics. The industry makes a significant contribution to the global economy and presents numerous opportunities for corporations to participate in this growing market (Akram, 2022). There are economic advantages to halal certification, including enhanced export opportunities, increased foreign investment, and job creation. The certification is a guarantee of compliance with halal standards recognised internationally, thus allowing corporations to approach new markets and increase their exports. The certification also draws foreign investment, as nations with reliable halal certification systems are considered lucrative investment destinations. The halal industry’s growth accelerates job creation, spanning various sectors. In turn, this process supports the development of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) existing in the halal industry (Omar et al., 2022). These economic benefits further reflect the significance of halal certification and its potential effect on economic growth and development. To initiate the current research on halal certification, it is essential to assess and identify the existing gaps in the literature for future studies. Although bibliometric analyses have been previously conducted on halal certification research, there remains a dearth of a comprehensive thematic and bibliometric review specifically focusing on halal certification as an alternative source of economic growth. Although previous studies have explored various aspects of the literature on halal certification, it is worthwhile to examine the specific themes and trends associated with the unique position of halal certification within the extensive global halal industry. This study is different from previous works, such as Masood (2022), which focused on a limited time frame from 2004 to 2021 and examined 248 articles, and Fadhlina and Nor (2024), which examined only 252 articles from 2005 to 2021. Furthermore, it is vital to observe that neither article was published in Scopus- Multidiscip. Rev. (2026) 9:e2026062 Received: March 9, 2025 | Accepted: June 09, 2025 Hussin et al. (2026) 2 indexed journals. As such, this creates a large gap in understanding the historical development and evolution of studies in this particular area. To address this crucial research gap, the current study aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of the halal certification literature by extending the period from 2003 to 2022. This extended duration will enable a comprehensive examination of the growth, challenges, and advancements in halal certification as an alternative source of economic growth. It is hoped that this research will provide policymakers, researchers, and industry practitioners with relevant insights to update them on the unique features, potential opportunities, and emerging areas in this field of study. Furthermore, the research findings will contribute to the existing body of knowledge by identifying research gaps, proposing potential future research directions, and providing a detailed analysis of the scholarly landscape encompassing the global halal market. To summarise, the study’s extended time frame, the inclusion of a wider selection of articles, and the implementation of a detailed analysis will provide up-to-date insights and increase our understanding of the development, problems and possible opportunities for halal certification. This strategy aims to identify key research trends, assess their impact, highlight influential authors, institutions, and journals, pinpoint research gaps, and propose directions for future research in the field of halal certification. 2. Materials and Methods The bibliometric analysis aims to distinguish current research trends and the intellectual structure of the literature, which utilises mathematical and statistical methods to examine the scientific literature in a particular subject. In bibliometric analysis, statistical tools are applied to keyword statistics, author statistics, and journal statistics. It is divided into two parts as proposed by Donthu et al. (2021) in their bibliometric analysis toolkit. The first section examines performance analysis, while the second section focuses on the scientific mapping of the existing literature. In this paper, a bibliometric analysis is conducted to examine current studies on halal certification. The results of the bibliometric analysis on halal certification are presented in the next section using the methodology proposed by Donthu et al. (2021). A total of 401 documents were retrieved from the Scopus database using the keyword “halal certification” on 19 June 2023 from 2003 to mid-2023. By choosing the term "halal certification," we have specifically prioritised management systems that have been verified by a reputable halal certification organisation (Masood, 2022). The Scopus database has a wider coverage of journals as compared to Web of Science, and was used due to its lower likelihood of article omissions compared to other databases (Singh et al., 2021). From the retrieved data, no duplicate documents were found, resulting in 401 unique documents. To ensure the relevance of the selected articles, all peer-reviewed documents published in English were included. The mentioned articles covered diverse fields of study categorised in the Scopus database from 2003 to 2022. This specific search yielded a final selection of 359 documents, chosen to provide the most accessible and readily available data. The year 2023 was excluded from the analysis, and this ensured a more comprehensive and reliable dataset. This is because the data for the particular year might not be complete or fully available in databases like Scopus. The task of manually analysing each article was given to two independent researchers to determine its suitability for the research scope. A thorough examination was conducted to filter out several articles which did not meet the research scope. This resulted in the exclusion of 5 articles. Thus, the selection for the final analysis was a total of 354 published documents. This number of documents was considered sufficient for implementing the bibliometric analysis (Rogers et al., 2020). The Bibliometrix package of R-tool (Aria & Cuccurullo, 2017) was utilised through the biblioshiny software for data visualisation. The software assists in conducting effective analysis on bibliometrics, emphasising co-citations, co-words, scientific collaboration, and coupling analysis (Biancone et al., 2020). The statistical analysis in this research enables the examination of current research on halal certification. The results were interpreted through performance analysis and science mapping, focusing on the main authors, journals, keywords, citations, articles, co-occurrences, bibliographic coupling, and co- citations. These results were acquired after conducting data cleaning and harmonisation processes (Kushairi & Ahmi, 2021). 3. Results 3.1. Performance analysis As shown in Figure 1, the early stages of research on halal certification (2003-2010) were characterised by limited scholarly attention and awareness, resulting in a relatively low number of published articles. This was the initial exploration phase, and scholars and researchers were beginning to understand halal certification and its possible effect on economic development. This period could be considered the beginning of the field, with scholars laying the groundwork for future exploration and establishing a foundation for further research. Significantly, Riaz and Choudry conducted early research on halal certification in 2003 and 2004, while Riaz (2007) and Che Man et al. (2007) expanded on this study by concentrating on halal verification and certification processes. The second phase of 2011 to 2015 showed a noticeable increase in interest and recognition of halal certification as an important topic of study. This period witnessed a growing number of published articles, with a remarkable surge in 2015. This https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Hussin et al. (2026) 3 indicated an increasing awareness of the economic impacts of halal certification. Scholars and researchers started to explore deeper into its possible advantages and impacts for various industries and markets, focusing on its growing importance as an alternative avenue for economic development. Additionally, halal certification represents the symbol of halal integrity and is required by importing countries to fulfil consumer demands (Masood, 2022). The period from 2016 to 2022 was a time when research on halal certification entered a phase of expansion and maturation. There was a consistent upward trend regarding the number of articles published, thus signifying a flourishing research landscape. Research output appeared to peak in 2020, with a significant number of articles published. This further reflected the strong interest and significance of the topic. Though the number of articles slightly decreased in the following years, they remained at a high volume, indicating a mature stage in the area of halal certification. During this period, researchers gathered extensive knowledge and established a growing understanding of the economic potential and impact of halal certification. To summarise, studies on halal certification as an alternative source of economic growth have gone through different phases. They began with a limited scholarly focus and steadily gained increased interest and recognition. Eventually, the study area widened and matured, drawing attention to substantial research activity and providing a much detailed insight into the economic implications of halal certification. (2026) 9 As seen in Figure 8, there are three distinct phases in the thematic evolution of the research on halal certification. In the first phase (2003-2017), the emphasis was on establishing trust and ensuring safety in halal-certified products. Particular themes emerged in this phase, such as consumer protection, counter-hegemony, and food safety. This reflected the efforts taken to create a dependable certification system which fulfils the needs of consumers. In addition, halal certification itself was a dominant theme, signifying the increasing recognition and importance of halal standards in the market. In the second phase (2018-2020), we witnessed a change towards understanding consumer behaviour and investigating the market potential of halal products. Particular themes became popular during this phase, such as consumer behaviour, Islamic marketing, and the halal market.. Scholars began to look into the preferences, attitudes, and purchasing patterns of Muslim consumers, thus acknowledging the need to fulfil the customers’ specific requirements. The emphasis widened beyond certification alone to include the larger aspects of the halal industry, such as market dynamics and consumer demand. In the third phase (2021-2022), halal certification research entered a period of diversification and investigated various applications within different industries. In this phase, specific themes emerged, such as halal tourism, halal cosmetics, and supply chain management. This highlighted the widening scope of halal certification beyond traditional food products. In this phase, the focus was on the significance of diversifying halal offerings and discovering new markets and industries. The dominant studies in this phase reflected the possible economic opportunities and growth which could be attained by integrating halal standards and practices in various sectors. The three phases generally display the growth of halal certification research, beginning with the establishment of trust and safety, then the shift towards understanding consumer behaviour and market potential, and lastly, looking into diversification and industry applications. The research conducted within each phase provides a thorough understanding of the halal certification ecosystem. Each research phase also provides awareness into possible repercussions as well as prospects for corporations operating in this field. Figure 8 Thematic Evolution. Source: Scopus database 3.2.3. Thematic Analysis and Discussions Four prevailing themes could be retrieved based on the thematic maps and evolution analysis. They are (1) established halal market and consumer trends, (2) consumer behaviour in halal certification, (3) halal industry growth strategies and assurance systems, and (4) halal certification in tourism. These dominant themes indicate that there is a widening influence of halal certification existing in multiple disciplines, thus suggesting significant implications in fields such as business, policy, technology, and cultural studies. 4.1. Established halal market and consumer trends Presently, we witness the evolution of the halal market from being a niche religious requirement to an international economic power. Factors such as the increasing Muslim population, combined with growing consciousness of food safety and ethical consumption, have been pivotal in magnifying the halal market to include non-Muslim customers who relate the term halal with hygiene, quality, and sustainability (Zafar et al., 2025). It is projected that the halal market will exceed USD 3.2 trillion by 2024 (Nor et al., 2023), including not only food products but also other products such as pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, fashion, and logistics. Current studies acknowledge halal certification as an important element of the ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) agenda. Customers now associate their buying habits with principles such as transparency and ethical sourcing, areas where halal certification plays a substantial role (Putri, 2024). Nations such as Malaysia and the UAE have taken advantage of this aspect by marketing themselves as international halal hubs. 4.2. Consumer behaviour in halal certification A vibrant research area in halal certification studies is consumer behaviour. Conventionally, religious obligation was the main determining factor of halal consumption (Yani & Suryaningsih, 2019). Nonetheless, recent studies have focused on the increasing effect of marketing, branding, peer networks and social media (Kamarulzaman et al., 2020). In the case of Muslim youths, it has been observed that they are gradually influenced by online influencers and visual brand cues rather than just religious devotion. Moreover, the non-Muslim consumer base is becoming increasingly important. According to Aziz and Chok (2013) and Rezai et al. (2012), halal-certified products are accepted by non-Muslims for their perceived healthy values, cleanliness, and ethical assurances. The rising halal appeal shows a combination of faith-based and value-based consumerism, implying that halal certification has grown into an international trusted brand. The utilisation of digital technology further transforms this shape. The analysis of AI-based sentiment implies that customer trust in halal certification is greatly influenced by online narratives and user-generated content (Azwar & Usman, 2025). As such, this indicates that in future, digital reputation management is indeed pivotal to halal branding strategies. 4.3. Halal industry growth strategies and assurance systems From the bibliometric map, we can ascertain one particular theme emerging, which is the requirement for robust halal assurance systems to reinforce market growth. As more companies enter the halal space—from logistics to biotechnology— the need for transparent, traceable, and technologically advanced certification mechanisms strengthens. Blockchain technology is being utilised to enable real-time traceability across halal supply chains (Karyani et al., 2024). This minimises fraud and also develops customer confidence in the integrity of the halal label. Nonetheless, an enduring challenge is the lack of international standardisation in halal certification. Diverse certification criteria and institutional fragmentation are disadvantageous for cross-border trade and may confuse consumers (Ghazali et al., 2023). Current studies propose a certification framework coordinated by international governance, such as the OIC/SMIIC 1: 2011, UAE.S/GSO 2055-1:2015, MS 1500:2009, MUIS-HC-S001, HAS 23000 (Lutfika et al., 2022). This unification would simplify processes, reduce redundancy, and increase global halal certification. 4.4. Halal certification in tourism Halal tourism, or Muslim-friendly tourism, signifies one of the most vibrant additions of halal certification. This sector combines religious values with travel and hospitality experiences, including aspects such as halal food availability, prayer facilities, privacy considerations, and culturally sensitive services. Initially, this tourism sector was dominated by Muslim- majority countries. However, non-Muslim countries such as Japan, South Korea, and Thailand have also joined the halal tourism sector to expand their tourism portfolios (Hasan et al., 2023). In this context, the certification role has two functions: it guarantees tourists of religious compliance and also acts as a marketing strategy to attract Muslim travellers. Current advancements include the usage of mobile apps for halal travel planning, digital maps of halal facilities, and AI-powered customer service tools personalised for Muslim tourists (Battour et al., 2023). Nonetheless, experts claim that inconsistencies in halal certification for tourism services across regions could obstruct sector growth. A standardised, internationally recognised halal tourism framework may reveal new economic prospects and promote Muslim travel experiences globally. 5. Research Gaps and Directions for Future Research https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Hussin et al. (2026) 12 To conclude, this study offers substantial evidence for examining different elements of halal certification. This review focuses on the potential research gaps and directions for further research in this area. Therefore, we identify four research gaps and directions for future research in the field of halal certification as an alternative source of economic growth: 1) Current research lacks detailed segmentation of the halal market, innovation in products beyond food and beverages, and exploration of regional cultural impacts on consumer trends. Future research should focus on advanced market segmentation to better understand diverse Muslim consumer groups, explore innovation in less-studied halal product categories such as cosmetics and pharmaceuticals, and conduct cross-regional analyses to investigate how cultural variations influence consumer preferences and trends. 2) There is limited research on the influence of digital media on consumer perceptions, the factors that build or erode trust in halal certification bodies, and the application of behavioural economics to purchasing decisions. Future studies should examine the impact of digital marketing and social media on consumer behaviour, investigate trust factors in halal certification processes, and apply behavioural economics principles to understand and improve marketing strategies for halal products. 3) Research gaps include challenges and solutions related to the standardisation of halal certification, integration of advanced technologies in assurance systems, and the cost-effectiveness of robust halal assurance systems. Future research should explore global standardisation efforts for halal certification, investigate the use of technologies like blockchain to enhance transparency and efficiency in assurance systems, and conduct cost-benefit analyses to understand the economic implications of comprehensive halal assurance systems. 4) Current studies lack comprehensive insights into the travel experience of Muslim tourists, the economic impact of halal tourism on local economies, and the standardisation of certification processes in the tourism industry. Future research should focus on investigating the holistic travel experience of Muslim tourists, including accommodation and leisure activities, studying the economic benefits and challenges of halal tourism for local communities, and developing and refining certification processes specific to halal tourism to ensure consistency and reliability across different regions and service providers. 6. Concluding Remarks This bibliometric analysis of research on halal certification as a driver of economic growth has illuminated the multifaceted and interdisciplinary nature of this field. The analysis highlights key themes such as established halal market and consumer trends, consumer behaviour in halal certification, halal industry growth strategies and assurance systems, and halal certification in tourism. The findings demonstrate the significant role of halal certification in promoting consumer trust, market expansion, and economic growth. However, several research gaps and areas for future exploration have been identified, including the need for advanced market segmentation, innovation in less-studied halal product categories, and comprehensive studies on consumer behaviour. Additionally, there is a need for comparative studies on the standardisation of halal certification, the integration of advanced technologies in assurance systems, and the economic impact of halal tourism. Addressing these gaps will enhance the understanding and effectiveness of halal certification practices, contributing to socio- economic development and the well-being of the community. JSON: Name: halal_standardization_econ_bibliometrics Title: Longitudinal bibliometric mapping combined with panel econometric analysis to measure the effect of halal certification standardization on halal-sector exports and foreign direct investment Short Hypothesis: Increased national-level harmonization of halal certification standards causes a statistically significant rise in halal-sector export volumes and inward foreign direct investment within three years of harmonization adoption. Related Work: Existing work divides into two streams: (1) descriptive and bibliometric studies that map research, themes, authors, and regional activity in halal certification, and (2) domain studies addressing consumer behaviour, certification procedures, traceability technologies (e.g., blockchain), and sectoral case studies (food, cosmetics, tourism). Bibliometric analyses to date are limited by short time windows, single-database sampling, and focus on intellectual structure rather than linking scholarly activity to economic outcomes. Empirical economic studies typically analyze demand-side drivers (consumer attitudes, marketing, halal tourism) or technical verification methods (PCR, traceability) but rarely quantify macroeconomic effects of certification standardization across countries. Proposed technological solutions demonstrate traceability improvements but lack evidence of measurable cross-border trade or investment impacts. Prior work therefore lacks (a) a reproducible, comparable metric of certification harmonization; (b) integrated analyses that combine bibliometric indicators with national economic outcomes; and (c) robust causal inference (panel/IV/DID) testing whether standard harmonization produces measurable export or FDI gains. Abstract: This study addresses whether harmonization of halal certification standards produces measurable economic benefits for halal-producing countries. We combine longitudinal bibliometric mapping of global halal-certification research with country-level panel econometric analysis to test whether increases in standard harmonization lead to higher halal-sector export volumes and greater inward foreign direct investment. Main contributions are (1) a reproducible harmonization index derived from standard adoption, mutual recognition agreements, and accreditation records; (2) integration of bibliometric indicators (research intensity, thematic diversity, centrality) as controls for knowledge-capacity; and (3) causal inference using panel fixed effects, difference-in-differences around harmonization events, and dynamic panel estimators. Expected outcomes include quantified elasticity of exports and FDI with respect to harmonization, evidence on time lags to impact, and an empirically grounded prioritization of policy levers. Results will inform policymakers and industry stakeholders on the economic returns to pursuing internationally harmonized halal certification. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Bibliometric corpus: Scopus export of publications matching "halal certification" and related keywords, 2003–2022; metadata: authors, affiliations, keywords, citations. (2) Economic outcomes: country-year halal-sector export volumes from UN Comtrade (HS codes mapped to halal-relevant categories), 2003–2022; country-year inward FDI in food/cosmetics/related sectors from World Bank/UNCTAD, 2003–2022. (3) Standardization inputs: country-year records of adopted halal standards (MS, GSO, OIC/SMIIC, MUIS, HAS), mutual recognition agreements (MRAs) count, number of accredited halal certifiers per country, year of major harmonization events from public registries and government reports. (4) Control variables: GDP, population, Muslim population share, global trade openness, logistics performance index, blockchain adoption indicator for supply chains. Preprocessing: harmonize country names, deflate monetary figures to constant USD, map HS codes to halal sectors, create panel with balanced coverage for N≈60 countries, T≈20 years where available. Variables: dependent = log(halal_exports+1), log(halal_FDI+1); main regressor = HarmonizationIndex (constructed as weighted sum of MRAs, international standard adoptions, accredited bodies per capita; normalized 0–1). Bibliometric regressors: research_intensity (publications per million pop), thematic_diversity (Shannon entropy of keywords), centrality_score (country affiliation eigenvector centrality in co-authorship network). Baselines: (A) pooled OLS without HarmonizationIndex, (B) country and year fixed effects (FE) without bibliometric controls, (C) FE with HarmonizationIndex, (D) dynamic Arellano-Bond with lagged dependent variables, (E) difference-in-differences (DID) using discrete harmonization adoption events, (F) IV regression using instrument = lagged regional harmonization rate or OIC membership*year interaction. Estimation and inference: clustered standard errors by country, heteroskedasticity-robust; p<0.05 significance. Evaluation metrics: coefficient estimates and 95% CIs for HarmonizationIndex, elasticity (percent change in dependent per 0.1 change in index), R-squared (within), AIC/BIC for model selection, Hansen test for IV validity, Arellano-Bond AR(2) test. Robustness and ablation: (1) remove bibliometric regressors to measure incremental explanatory power; (2) alternative HarmonizationIndex constructions (equal weights, PCA-based); (3) exclude high-leverage countries (top exporters) and re-estimate; (4) include blockchain_adoption dummy and test interaction HarmonizationIndex*blockchain. Network and bibliometric analyses: co-authorship and co-word networks using Louvain community detection, modularity scores, node centralities (betweenness, eigenvector), temporal topic modeling (LDA) with coherence metric; compute correlations between bibliometric metrics and HarmonizationIndex. Pre-registered checks: placebo tests using pre-adoption pseudo-events, Granger-causality tests with 3-year lags, and out-of-sample prediction RMSE for 5-year windows. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement error in HarmonizationIndex due to incomplete or inconsistent public records of MRAs and accreditor registries; misclassification of HS codes as halal-relevant causing outcome noise; endogeneity and reverse causality (higher exports may motivate harmonization) leading to biased estimates if instruments are weak; limited temporal lag identification if economic effects occur beyond the study window; coverage bias from Scopus (underrepresentation of regional journals) affecting bibliometric controls; omitted variable bias from unobserved policy or geopolitical shocks; heterogeneity across product categories and countries that limits generalization of a single elasticity; small-sample problems for DID if few harmonization events occur; computational scalability for large network/topic models when expanding corpus beyond Scopus; legal and definitional heterogeneity in what constitutes "harmonization" across jurisdictions.
